2.heading: In this lecture
2.why: the title block was the deck title plus its reading; Schell Ch. 10, 11, 18 is in the credit line

3.heading: Flow
bullets: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, a psychologist, set out to identify the elements of enjoyment across different people and activities
He found that enjoyment is described the same:
the world over, regardless of age, gender, social class, culture
across activities – playing music, chess, sports, painting
Flow is an experience “so gratifying that people are willing to do it for its own sake, with little concern for what they will get out of it, even when it is difficult or dangerous”
The goal is an excuse for the process
3.why: nothing dropped; the definition and its gloss move to their own slide so the quotation fits

4.heading: The conditions for flow
bullets: a task that can be completed
the ability to concentrate on the task
concentration is possible because the task has clear goals
concentration is possible because the task provides immediate feedback
the ability to exercise a sense of control over actions
a deep but effortless involvement that removes awareness of the frustrations of everyday life
concern for self disappears, but sense of self emerges stronger afterwards
the sense of the duration of time is altered

4.why: Csikszentmihalyi's eight conditions are kept word for word and broken across two slides; the heading no longer repeats “Flow”

5.heading: Skill-challenge balance
bullets: Skill-challenge balance is central
Too high challenge – frustration
Too low challenge – boredom
Aiming to keep the player in the “flow channel”
Represents overall skill-challenge balance
Not moment-to-moment pacing

5.why: nothing dropped; the source's “-->” arrows become dashes

6.heading: GameFlow
bullets: A model of player enjoyment in video games: 38 criteria, 8 elements
Maps to Csikszentmihalyi’s concept of flow
Criteria derived from games UX/PX literature
Heuristics for design and evaluation
Widely cited (>3000) and used (>200) – games and game-like experiences
Concentration
Challenge
Player Skills
Control
Clear Goals
Feedback
Immersion
Social Interaction
6.why: the nine-row GAMEFLOW table did not fit beside the list and the Sweetser & Wyeth reference; its eight elements are written out as the second slide

7.heading: GameFlow Affordances
bullets: Seven affordances rather than elements: game designers do not directly create gameplay experiences
The experience exists between the player and the game
No specific or prescriptive criteria, only high-level affordances
7.why: the first sentence's second half becomes its own sub-bullet; nothing dropped

8.heading: How the elements map
bullets: Involvement captures Concentration and Immersion: attention-demanding tasks and sensory stimuli
Skill-Challenge Balance maps to the central corresponding component of flow
Learning & Mastery captures the integration of learning and play, and the need for mastery and reward
Control & Agency includes lower-level and direct control, plus choice and meaningful impact in the game
Goals & Progression includes Clear Goals, and Feedback in terms of progression
Comfort & Safety relates to the player’s connection to an external influence, their environment
8.why: each sentence becomes a fragment led by its affordance; “(i.e., tasks)” and “(i.e., stimuli)” lose the hedge. Comfort & Safety came from the same source slide and stays with it

9.heading: The seven affordances
bullets: Involvement — engages the player cognitively, physically and emotionally with satisfying tasks and stimuli (quality, quantity, variety)
Skill-Challenge Balance — for different players and throughout the game; progression is bi-directional, rising skill driving challenge and rising challenge driving skill
Learning & Mastery — learning and play integrated seamlessly; the player can demonstrate mastery and is rewarded appropriately
Control & Agency — control of movement, interaction, interface, controls and play sessions; agency over actions, strategies and impact on the world, with feedback on both
Goals & Progression — overarching and intermediate goals clearly presented, or set by the player, with feedback on progress and status
Comfort & Safety — play space, body position, movement and wellness, for different players and throughout the session
Social Interaction — social play (competition, cooperation, observation) and social connection, inside and outside the game

split_image.alt: An adult steadying a small child on a balance bike: challenge matched to skill, where falling is safe.

9.why: Sweetser & Ozdowska's seven definitions were a two-column table the converter flattened into seven paragraph-long bullets; they are kept in full, one bullet each, across three slides, with the repeated “The game affords” stem dropped

12.heading: Self-Determination Theory (SDT)
bullets: Explains motivation based on innate psychological needs
Competence – need for challenge and feelings of effectance
I need to feel good at something
Autonomy – sense of volition or willingness
I need freedom to do things my own way
Relatedness – sense of belonging and connectedness to others
I need to connect with other people
Satisfying the needs can enhance intrinsic motivation
Intrinsic motivation: doing something because it is inherently interesting or enjoyable
Behaviours people often do for no external reward: play, exploration, challenge seeking
Extrinsic motivation: doing something because it leads to a separable outcome

12.why: the four loose text boxes (Ryan & Deci's definitions of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation) were hidden in a comment and are restored as the second slide; the DOI is already in the credit line, so the link bullet goes

13.heading: #22 The Lens of Needs
bullets: On which levels of Maslow's hierarchy is my game operating?
Does it fill the needs of competence, autonomy, and relatedness?
How can I make my game fill more basic needs than it already does?
For the needs my game is already filling, how can it fill those needs even better?
What motivations do players have to play my game?
Which motivations are most internal? Which are most external?
Which are pleasure seeking? Which are pain avoiding?
Which motivations support each other?
Which motivations are in conflict?
13.why: two lenses shared one source slide; every question is kept word for word and the second lens takes its own heading instead of “(cont.)”

15.heading: Gamification and gameful design
bullets: Design strategy of using game design elements in non-game contexts
Selection and usage of the game design elements is key
Can play to intrinsic or extrinsic motivation
Play is central to games: rules and goals alone do not make a game
Meaningful gamification – using game design elements to build intrinsic motivation and meaning in non-game settings
Points, levels, leaderboards, achievements
Rewards can undermine or damage intrinsic motivation
Can be experienced as more or less controlling
Leaderboards can be experienced as goal setting
Game platform achievements can be competence or ego boosts
15.why: “Meaningful gamification” and its definition are one bullet; “Reward-based gamification” was a label on the source slide and becomes the second slide's heading
